name: Trió
sweep_summary: Trió is not in the catalog. The sweep's two items are one paper: Meira 1998 'Rhythmic Stress in Tiriyó (Cariban)', IJAL 64(4): 352-378, DOI 10.1086/466366 (Glottolog 93167 is a duplicate from Fabre's bibliography with the author wrongly given as Edmundo Magaña; Crossref confirms Meira). The article is paywalled and could not be fetched sources (no OA copy per Semantic Scholar; publisher/JSTOR 403; not on archive.org/HathiTrust). Its analysis is available first-hand in Meira's open Rice dissertation (1999, hdl 1911/19417, already on file under salu1254 and now linked into trio1238), pages 60 and 63 read directly from renders: iambic rhythmic stress, final syllable never stressed, every non-final heavy syllable stressed, every second light syllable from the word start or the nearest heavy syllable stressed, no primary stress identified (p. 71), length not pitch as the cue (p. 70). Meira 2006 ELL2 (on file) repeats this as 'weight-sensitive rhythmic (iambic) stress' citing Meira 1998. Recommended catalog coding for a new record: rhythmic/iambic, weight-sensitive, left-to-right, final extrametrical, no culminative primary stress. Still worth acquiring: Meira 1998 IJAL (high, paywalled) and Carlin 2004 A Grammar of Trio (print only) as an independent second description.

new_statements.quote: The following rules summarize the various facts described above, giving an overall characterization of Tiriyó rhythmic stress in terms of (C)V ('light') or non-(C)V ('heavy') syllables. (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. [p. 63] ... there seems to be no reason to analyze any single syllable in a phonological word as bearing primary stress. [p. 71]
new_statements.citation: Meira, Sérgio. 1999. A Grammar of Tiriyó. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston. §2.5.1 Rhythmic stress, pp. 60-72.
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive iambic rhythmic stress from the left edge: in all-light words the 2nd, 4th, 6th... syllables are stressed and the final syllable is always unstressed (so all-light bisyllables get no lengthened stress, only a pitch drop, pp. 66-67); every non-final heavy syllable (coda, VV, VVh, VVN) is stressed and restarts the alternation; no primary (culminative) stress is identified; the phonetic cue is vowel length, not pitch (p. 70). Stress shifts with prefixation (pakoro [pa.kó:.ro] 'house' vs ji-pakoro [ji.pá:.ko.ro] 'my house', p. 62). First-hand, from extensive fieldwork; expanded version of the IJAL 1998 analysis.

sources.note: Title and Meira's own citation of it (ELL2 2006 p. 201: 'Many languages have weight-sensitive rhythmic (iambic) stress (Table 1; Meira, 1998)') make this the journal statement of Tiriyó iambic rhythmic stress; the article itself was not readable: Crossref lists no license, Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 143440293) shows closed access with no OA PDF, publisher and JSTOR pages return 403, not on archive.org or HathiTrust full view. Its content is presumably the same analysis as Meira 1999 §2.5.1 (open, read here).
